en: An Essential Summary of the Exegesis of the Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom,
Citing the Exegeses of Various Masters;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Commentary by the Tang Dynasty National Master Faxiang; Sub-commentary by the Song Dynasty Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gushan;
Annotations by the Yuan Dynasty Śramaṇa Yuàncuì of Gǔyún; Annotations by the Yuan Dynasty Śramaṇa Xiàngzhèng;
and Explanatory Commentary by Zōnglè, Abbot of the Tianjie Chan Temple during the Ming Dynasty, in fulfillment of Imperial Decree.
The Great Ming Hanlin Academician Qianxi Zong Jingliao composed these words:
"Buddha" means awakening; it is the awakening to one's own nature (*svabhāva*). Its dharma proceeds from precepts to meditative concentration and then to wisdom.
It does not cling to external forms, nor does it cling to internal emptiness. It is the true vision of one's original face—empty yet luminous, essential and subtle, pure and perfectly integrated.
Only then can one apply the undefiled state to resolve the great public case of transcending the world.

Furthermore, out of compassion for sentient beings whose worldly defilements are heavy and whose roots of affliction are deep—often mistaking thieves for children and delusion for truth—he preached this sutra to liberate them.
Its prose is archaic, its meaning profound, and its language concise.
Its essential purport is comprehensive and leaves nothing out; while dwelling in leisurely seclusion, I took pleasure in reading this sutra.

Finding the interpretations of various schools to be overly prolix, I have selected its most essential and precise passages and recorded them here, intending to await those who have attained the samādhi of the Buddha’s scriptures so that they may verify them.
Written by the Layman Wunian on the day after the full moon in the fifth month of summer in the Gui-si year of the Jiajing era, beneath the purple microcosm (Ziwēihuā).
Zongle said: "One should know that this sutra is the essential core of the great *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures spoken by the World-Honored One."
The teachings of the Bodhisattvas are identical to the teachings of the Buddha;

they have been transmitted to China through five translations, and we now follow that translated by Xuanzang because it is the most widely circulated in the Middle Kingdom. *Prajñā* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "wisdom.
*Pāramitā* is a Chinese term meaning "reaching the other shore. Sentient beings, due to delusion regarding the nature of wisdom, dwell within the cycle of birth and death.
Death is called "this shore," and the Bodhisattva, through the cultivation of *prajñā*, awakens to the nature of wisdom and reaches *nirvāṇa*, which is called "the other shore.
The "mind" refers to the *prajñā*-mind; this *prajñā*-mind is inherently possessed by every person.
One who preaches this sutra does so with the desire to cause sentient beings to sever deluded minds and manifest their original nature. "Sutra" means "Dharma" and "constancy."

This sutra takes a single dharma as its name, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence, contemplative insight (*pratyavekṣā*) as its primary tenet, the crossing over suffering as its function, and the Mahāyāna as its teaching.
These five points are all the essential purports explained within the sutra. "The single dharma" refers to the *prajñāpāramitā*;
"the true mark" refers to the empty nature of all phenomena; "contemplative insight" refers to...
"To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty" means to transcend suffering;
"to transcend all suffering and calamity" is the profound *prajñā* practiced by Bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna.
Worthy One, it is said that Prajñā is the essence; this is translated as "wisdom," which refers to the spiritual awakening to profound mysteries and the subtle realization of the true source.

Pāramitā is the function; this is translated as "reaching the other shore," meaning that by means of this wondrous wisdom, one overturns the cycle of birth and death, exhausts all transgressions, and arrives at the limit of true emptiness.
Guyu said: "This wisdom is free from discursive thought; its universal awakening is utterly perfect. It is form and it is emptiness; it is neither arising nor ceasing.
To turn one's back on it, the path of the mind is suddenly severed; to employ it, the Dharma-realm is fully encompassed.

Thus, through this wondrous wisdom, one crosses from this shore of birth-and-death, traverses the middle current of afflictions, and reaches the other shore of Nirvana. What is this Nirvana? It is realization."
Birth and death are this sūtra; it is the mark of emptiness of all dharmas. Because all delusions are empty, it is called the "True Mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
To manifest the essence and illuminate the principle is precisely "perfect illumination. As the sūtra says, "By practicing deeply in prajñā, one sees that the five aggregates are all empty.

This emptiness is the actual substance. Taking this substance as the basis to give rise to illumination is "perfect illumination"; by means of perfect illumination, one reunites with the substance. Yet, the substance itself is not a substantial reality.
If they illuminate one another, they do not constitute complete illumination; if there is no complete illumination, the true mark (*dharmatā*) does not exist.
Fohai said: "This is the core essence of the six hundred fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which is why it is called the 'Heart Sūtra.
It is not the mind of wisdom, nor the mind of grass and trees, nor the physical heart of flesh. However, the substance of this mind is quiescent yet illuminating, empty yet harmonious."
The spiritual brilliance is penetratingly clear, encompassing both the mundane and the sagely; truth and falsehood share a common source. The translation by [Feng] contains no superfluous words;
it is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit original. From "Avalokiteśvara" down to "deliverance from all suffering and calamity" constitutes the introductory preface (*nidāna*) and its thematic intent.
It is also said to briefly mark out the essential framework, or to indicate the commencement based on practice. From "Śāriputra, form is not different [from emptiness]"...
From "Emptiness" down to "Supreme Perfect Enlightenment," this section clarifies the true doctrine of emptiness.
Song Jingliao said: "It gathers all myriad virtues back into the source of the mind and penetrates the very marrow of the various sutras.
This sutra establishes its title through seven aspects; this particular one is established based on both the Dharma and a metaphor. In the Sanskrit language, *prajñā*; here it is translated as...
"Wisdom" (*prajñā*) in the Sanskrit language means "perfection" (*pāramitā*); *pāra* here translates as "the other shore," and *mita* translates as "to reach.

In the common parlance of the Western lands (India), that which signifies the completion of a task is called "the other shore. Because the Buddha was born in that land, he adopted this vernacular term to clarify his teachings;
thus, "this shore" refers to sentient beings performing karma in this turbid world, undergoing suffering within the cycle of birth and death.
The "ground" refers to the realm of ultimate liberation, purity, and supreme bliss attained by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
the "mind" refers to the general characteristic of all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane. Specifically, there are five types:
first, the "fleshly heart," which resembles a plantain bud, arises within the physical body, and is categorized as insentient matter; second, the "discursive mind," which resembles...

1. Wild fires that suddenly arise and suddenly extinguish are categorized as *vikalpa* (delusive conceptualization); 2. The state of the gathering mind resembles seeds hidden within grass; this is categorized as *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies); 3.
The state of the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) resembles a fertile field where fine seeds grow without end; this is categorized as *avidyā* (ignorance); 4.
The state of the *tathatā-citta* (mind of suchness) is like empty space, vast and encompassing the entire *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm); this is *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (quiescence and insight).
Regarding the summary of this sutra’s title as the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya* (The Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom):
it means that if a person can sever emotional attachments and conceptualizations through wisdom—like a boatman who steers a vessel across to the other shore—they will finally understand this heart.
This sutra concludes its final chapter with the term "mind," revealing only the single character "one mind"; this is a skillful feature of its literary style.

This sutra speaks only of upward attainment and not of downward study; for its practical cultivation, one should consult the three sutras: the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and the *Amitāyurdhyāna* (or *Mahāsaṃnipāta*).
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, Zongle said:
"The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is a bodhisattva capable of cultivating *prajñā*.
*Prajñāpāramitā* is the dharma cultivated by the bodhisattva. The bodhisattva employs the wisdom of contemplation (*prajñā-darśana-jñāna*)."
Because one illuminates and realizes that one’s own mind is pure, perfectly interfused, and unimpeded, it is called "self-mastery" (*svatantra*); this is self-benefit.

Furthermore, by reflecting upon sentient beings in the world who undergo suffering, causing them to practice this Dharma so that they may reform evil and transform toward goodness, and thereby leave suffering behind to attain happiness, there is no lack of mastery;
this is benefiting others. "Bodhisattva" is a Sanskrit term for *bodhisattva*.
In the language of China, "Awakening Beings" (Jue Zhongsheng) is abbreviated as simply "Bodhisattva. "Practice" (xing) refers to cultivation;
"profound Prajñā" (shen banruo) refers to the Prajñā of the True Mark (shixiang banruo). Because it is not something observed by those of coarse minds or shallow wisdom, it is called "profound.
"Time" (shi) refers to the time when the Bodhisattva practices Prajñā. Xianshou says: "The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara."
This means that because one attains mastery in contemplating and penetrating the unimpeded realm of phenomena and principles, this name is established.
*Bodhi* is called "awakening" (*jue*); *sattva* is called "sentient beings" (*zhòngshēng*). There are two kinds of the sublime practice of *prajñā*:
first, the shallow, which is the *prajñā* of entering emptiness; second, the deep, which is the *prajñā* of the emptiness of dharmas. As for the Bodhisattvas...
The term "Dharma Prince" (*dharmarāja-putra*) is a general designation. As for "Deep Prajñā," it exhausts the source and reaches the ultimate limit.
Song Jingliao stated: *Bodhi* here means "awakening" (*bodha*), and *sattva* means "sentient being" (*sattva*).

A sentient being is one who possesses a living soul; while "sentient beings" refers to those with life, they are called "sentient beings" because even grasses and trees possess birth but lack [sentience].
All sentient beings who possess Buddha-nature are "sentient beings with feelings" (*sattva-saṃjñin*);
however, because only Bodhisattvas among these sentient beings have attained awakening, they are called "Awakened Sentient Beings" (*bodhisattva*).
"Clearly seeing that the five aggregates are all empty, one transcends all suffering and affliction.
Zongle said: "To 'clearly see' (zhào) means to contemplate. The 'five aggregates' (wǔ yùn) are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

'Aggregates' (yùn) means accumulation. 'Empty' (kōng) refers to true emptiness. 'Form' (sè) refers to the physical body. 'Sensation' (shòu) refers to reception and experience. 'Perception' (xiǎng) refers to..."

"Volition" (*saṃskāra*) refers to mental formations; "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to discrimination. Consciousness is the sovereign mind-king, while sensation, perception, and volition are the activities produced by the mind.
"Deliverance" means liberation. "All sufferings and calamities" refers to the manifold sufferings of the world.

Because the Bodhisattva perceives that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty and quiescent, he is freed from the suffering of birth and death; yet, he further takes pity on those who remain lost in delusion.
Sentient beings, through their inverted delusions, contravene principle and disrupt the natural order; by committing the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes, they undergo manifold sufferings.
Therefore, this Dharma-gate of Prajñāpāramitā is taught so that they may practice it and all attain liberation.
The preceding section is a narrative from the time Ānanda compiled the Dharma-treasury, describing the merit of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in delivering sentient beings.
The preceding section constitutes the separate introduction. From the point where Śāriputra begins in the following section, it is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s response to Śāriputra’s question.

Because the five aggregates are not empty in nature, they possess obstructions; being unable to be void, yet not being non-void, they lack spiritual efficacy. Thus, the five aggregates [are as described].
These [skandhas] do not belong to the original nature; since the five skandhas are empty, the original nature is naturally void and luminous.
It is like a mirror becoming bright when dust and grime are removed, or water becoming clear when silt and mud are cleared away.
That the ancients said Buddhists practice "universal love" (jien'ai) refers to this. Zhang Xujing said: "The Great Way is not far off."
Within the body, all physical forms are empty in nature; if they were not empty, the vital energy (*prāṇa*) would remain stagnant.
When the energy returns to the fundamental ocean, life becomes infinite.
Xianshou said: "While all minds are equally empty, those who contemplate only the five aggregates [do so] because of the physical form of all sentient beings."
Because the mind is constantly present, the initial contemplation of the realm of the aggregates (*skandhas*) in *śamatha-vipaśyanā* shares this same intent. As for "all are empty":
since form is created by the mind, the entirety of form is mind; and since the mind has only a name, how could form have any reality? Therefore, it is said that "all are empty."
Although all things are numerous, they do not transcend the two dharmas of mind and body; the body is the root of all suffering, and the mind is the source of all delusions.
If one cuts down a tree and reaches its root, all illusions will cease.

The *Yan famen jing* (Sūtra on the Gate of the Adorned Dharma) states: "The essential nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is itself the essential nature of all Buddhas.
Although a Bodhisattva manifests the afflictions of the five aggregates, they do not conjoin with those afflictions, for their essential nature is untainted.
Thus, although a Bodhisattva manifests the birth and death of the five aggregates to teach and transform sentient beings, they know that all dharmas have neither coming nor going."

Song Jingliao said: "The term 'skandha' (蘊) carries the meaning of 'containing' or 'encompassing. The five skandhas are form (rūpa), sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna).
The aggregate of form is composed of the four great elements. The aggregate of sensation refers to the experiencing of suffering, pleasure, and that which is neither painful nor pleasant.

The aggregate of perception refers to the grasping of various objects without ceasing to run toward them. The aggregate of mental formations consists of the various mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), many of which involve greed for objects and do not come to rest."

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) intensely discerns its objects; among the five aggregates, consciousness takes precedence because it is through this discernment that it experiences [objects] within the mind—this is called feeling (*vedanā*).
Once the mind has experienced them, there arises a continuous stream of investigation, which is called perception (*saṃjñā*).
When this perception is not yet exhausted, it proceeds to formative activity, which is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Sentient beings sink [into saṃsāra]...

Deluded by this, they do not realize it themselves, nor do they know that form is like a mass of foam, sensation is like a water bubble, perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like a magical illusion; these are not the true nature.

Only Bodhisattvas penetrate and see that the self-nature of the five aggregates is entirely empty—a profound principle of the two-fold emptiness perceived through wisdom. This "function" is like a sword.
It is also said that "equanimity" (*samatā*) refers to suffering and hardship; these are the various forms of suffering. Indeed, for one who is born, life is a vessel of suffering:
to be cold and lack clothing is suffering; to be hungry and lack food is suffering; to be weary and lack rest is suffering; to be ill and lack recovery is suffering.
Furthermore, there is what is called the suffering of association with the hated (*appiyasampayoga-dukkha*), such as when kinsmen quarrel and contend.
The suffering of separation from what is loved is like the death of one's own flesh and bone;
the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks is when whatever one strives for does not fulfill one's intentions;

the suffering of old age is when all faculties weaken while one vainly yearns for strength; and the suffering of death is when everything previously possessed is entirely abandoned. Yet, all these various sufferings...
The five aggregates are its cause. When a Bodhisattva realizes and perceives true emptiness, suffering and affliction are exhausted;
being far removed from the two kinds of birth and death—segmented and transformational—they attain bodhi and nirvana. Therefore, it is said that they "cross over all suffering and distress.
This first section states that the five aggregates are all empty, serving as the guiding framework for this entire sutra, which will be detailed in the following text.
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. (This is the contemplation of emptiness and the contemplation of illusion.)
Zongle said: "Śāriputra was a disciple of the Buddha whose wisdom was foremost.
Because he had questioned on behalf of the assembly, the Bodhisattva called him by name and addressed him: 'Form is the illusory form of the four great elements;
emptiness is the true emptiness of Prajñā. Sentient beings, through delusion regarding true emptiness, undergo illusory form, just as water forms ice.'"
Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas cultivate the wisdom of Prajñā-observation, they clearly perceive that illusory form is itself true emptiness;

it is like melting ice into water. Since the essence of form and emptiness is no different, it is said that "form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form," just as ice is not different from water and water is not different from ice. Yet, fearing that sentient beings of dull faculties [might misunderstand], [the Buddha further explained:]...
Because one has not yet fully realized [the truth], the two views of form and emptiness still persist; thus it is said that "form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Just as water is itself water and water is itself ice, so it is with sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—there is nothing that is not thus.
This is the essential point of this sutra, the very heart of Prajñāpāramitā.
This section should be understood in conjunction with the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*: "Whatever has marks is all false and illusory;
if one sees that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. This is to be compared with the passage on Nirvāṇa.
Xianshou said: "In the Hīnayāna, form is not emptiness; one must extinguish form for it to become empty. Now it is not so: form..."
This is emptiness; it is not the emptiness resulting from the extinction of form.
Yunqiao said: "Among the six sense objects, those to whom people are most prone to become attached are forms, followed by the others.
Therefore, the Buddha singled out this one word and spoke of it first."

Song Jingliao said: "That which has form is called 'form' (rūpa), and that which is formless is called 'emptiness' (śūnyatā). To say that form is not different from emptiness clarifies that form is but an illusion.
What is meant by 'form does not obstruct emptiness' is that if it were to obstruct emptiness, it would be substantial form rather than illusory form.
To say that emptiness is not different from form clarifies that emptiness is the manifestation of the single reality, and thus it must necessarily not be obstructed."
If form were obstructed by form, it would be a void of annihilation rather than true emptiness; this statement means that form and emptiness do not obstruct one another.
"Form is itself emptiness" clarifies that emptiness does not exist through the extinction of form. "Emptiness is itself form" clarifies that emptiness cannot be grasped as a separate entity.
This speaks to the non-duality of form and emptiness. In general, true emptiness is like a perfect circle.

A mirror reflects forms according to objects, yet within the mirror there has never been a form; this so-called "empty essence" (śūnyatā) is never absent, and it is through its presence that emptiness is discerned.
Illusory forms are like bubbles, shadows, lightning, or dew; at the very moment they appear, what form is not present?
Yet in a single kṣaṇa, they change and perish, no longer existing; this so-called "illusory existence" is [nevertheless] not absent.

The initial statement that "non-emptiness is itself emptiness" serves to clarify existence. As for the passage "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise," it should have been stated as:
"feeling is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from feeling; feeling is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself feeling.

The same applies to perception, mental formations, and consciousness—there is nothing that is not thus. However, fearing that the text would become overly prolix, it is abbreviated and simply states "likewise."
It is thus. This second section of three paragraphs explains in detail that the five aggregates are all empty.
Śāriputra, the mark of the emptiness of all dharmas is that they are neither produced nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Zongle said: "These 'dharmas' refer to the aforementioned five aggregates; their 'empty characteristic' is precisely the true characteristic of ultimate emptiness.

The Bodhisattva further addressed Śāriputra, saying: "Since one has realized that all dharmas are, in their very substance, the essence of the true characteristic of ultimate emptiness, they are fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
Since there is no arising or ceasing, how could there be defilement or purity? Since there is none..."
How could there be increase or decrease in defilement and purity?
This statement regarding the original nature of reality corresponds to what Mencius called the "fixed allotment" (*fen-ding*);
the true mark of ultimate emptiness is precisely the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).
Worthy One said: "Neither arising nor ceasing" refers to the stage prior to the Path, the position of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

it means that while ordinary beings undergo the cycle of death here and birth there, transmigrating through long kalpas, this is a state of arising and ceasing. Because true emptiness (*tattva-śūnyatā*) is free from this, it is called neither arising nor ceasing.
"Neither defiled nor pure" refers to the stages on the Path, such as those of the Bodhisattvas; it means that for all Bodhisattvas, the stains of the hindrances have not yet [been fully eliminated].
Having completed the practice of total purity, it is called the stage of "defilement and purity.

Because true emptiness transcends this, it is said to be "neither defiled nor pure" and "neither increasing nor decreasing. Within the stage of the Buddha-fruit after the Path, that which was previously not exhausted—namely the afflictions and obstacles of birth and death—is now exhausted;
this is "decrease. That which was previously not perfected through cultivation—the myriad virtues—is now perfected; this is "increase."
Because true emptiness is detached from these, it is said to neither increase nor decrease. When form arises from conditions, true emptiness does not arise;
when form ceases due to conditions, true emptiness does not perish. Furthermore, while following the flow [of phenomena], it is unstained; while emerging from hindrances, it is not exhausted.

When hindrances are exhausted, it does not diminish; when virtues are fulfilled, it does not increase. By reversing this to reveal the characteristic of true emptiness, it is called the "characteristic of emptiness."
Thus it is said. Mount Gu said: Because form is not different from emptiness, it is unborn; because emptiness is not different from form, it is unceasing;
because form is not different from emptiness, it is not defiled; because emptiness is not different from form, it is not pure; because form is not different from emptiness, it does not increase.
Because emptiness is not different from form, there is no diminution; because saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa, there is no arising; because nirvāṇa is itself saṃsāra, there is no cessation;
because afflictions are themselves bodhi, there is no defilement; because bodhi is itself affliction, there is no purity;
because fetters and karma are themselves liberation, there is no increase; because liberation is itself fetters and karma, there is no decrease.
Guyun said: Since the Dharma is eternally quiescent, from where could delusion arise? Because it does not admit even a single speck of dust, it is called the mark of emptiness;
that all delusions are empty is also called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Originally unborn, it is now unextinguished; afflictions are not defilement and nirvāṇa is not purity.
It does not increase when among the sages, nor does it decrease when among ordinary beings; it is ultimately equal and universally one.
"One who contemplates in this way in all places is identical to the Buddhas.

Song Jingliao said: "These three sections speak of the empty nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), beginning with their original absence of arising and ceasing, thereby fulfilling the meaning of the second section."
Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Zongle said: "Since within this true reality of ultimate emptiness there can be no arising or ceasing, defilement or purity, increase or decrease, it is summarized by saying 'no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. 'No' (wu) means emptiness."
Gu Yun said: "The wondrous emptiness is so thoroughly blended that it penetrates all phenomena within True Suchness (tathatā); it sweeps away even the single non-existence into ultimate reality.
Only this is the Prajñā-wisdom of Emptiness of the Perfect School.
Song Jinglan said: "Therefore, this follows from the preceding text. The 'emptiness within emptiness' is precisely the characteristic of emptiness (śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa)."
This emptiness is what is called "true emptiness. Within true emptiness, how could there be the evil of the five aggregates?
From this section up to the thirteen instances of the word "non-existent" in the passage "neither wisdom nor attainment," the literary structure is also extraordinary;
from the five aggregates through the twelve links of dependent origination and the four noble truths, all are utterly absent within the nature of the Bodhisattva.
However, as for the practical application of this work, one should examine the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, specifically the line:

"How does one subdue the mind? Otherwise, one must also examine the three contemplations, two obstacles, and four losses in the *Niyatāniyatagati-parivarta* (or *Yuanjue jing*) before one can fully comprehend these thirteen instances of the word "no" (*wu*).
"No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no眼界 (eye-element) up to and including no consciousness-element.
Zongle said: "Within the true reality of ultimate emptiness, there are also no six sense organs and six sense objects; this empties the twelve [bases]."

As for "entrance" (*āyatana*), there are neither the twelve entrances nor the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). The eighteen realms consist of the six sense organs, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses.
The phrase "and so forth" (*yāvat*) indicates the beginning and the end while omitting the middle;

as explained above, the five aggregates, twelve entrances, and eighteen realms do not transcend the two dharmas of form and mind. This is taught for those whose delusion regarding the mind is predominant.

The five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are taught for those whose delusion regarding form is predominant; the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana) are taught for those whose delusion regarding both form and mind is equal;

and the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu) are taught for others. Among these three categories, a practitioner who trains in them may enter into awakening by cultivating just one category, according to their individual faculties.
Fohai said: "The old term 'twelve entrances' (*āyatana*) refers to the six sense organs and six sense objects mutually entering one another.
The new term 'twelve bases' (*āyatana*) refers to the internal organs and external objects each having their own distinct locations and functions.

When practitioners use them daily, they realize that the essence of these organs and objects is itself *prajñā*, which is suddenly perfected as empty awareness; therefore, it is said to be 'non-existent'."
Song Jingliao said: "The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are called the six *indriyas* (roots), just as plants and trees have roots.
They are also called the six *āyatanas* (entrances); 'root' (*indriya*) refers to what is internal, while 'entrance' (*āyatana*) refers to what is external.

Seeing with the eye constitutes the dust of form; hearing with the ear constitutes the dust of sound; smelling with the nose constitutes the dust of fragrance; and tasting with the tongue constitutes the dust of flavor."

The physical body stained by touch becomes the dust of touch; the mind attached to phenomena becomes the dust of phenomena. These are called the six dusts (*ṣaḍ-rasa*), which are so named because they act as obstructions like grains of sand or dust.
The union of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their corresponding objects (*viṣaya*) constitutes the twelve bases (*āyatana*);

this means that each has its own specific location. From seeing arises eye-consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*); from hearing arises ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*); from smelling arises nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇa-vijñāna*).

Consciousness arising from tasting is the tongue-consciousness; arising from contact with defilement is the body-consciousness; and arising from discrimination is the mental consciousness—these are called the six consciousnesses.

"Consciousness" refers to the deluded production that discriminates and analyzes, thereby obscuring and clouding true wisdom. The union of these three [consciousness, object, and faculty] constitutes the eighteen *dhātus* (realms).
"*Dhātu*" means a limit; it signifies that each has its own distinct domain. The phrase "and so forth" (*nai zhi*) is an abbreviation; the preceding section has already raised this point.
From "there is no eye-element" downwards, one may understand the intermediate four consciousness-elements by analogy with the absence of the mind-consciousness-element.
The reason sentient beings are submerged in birth and death is that these three mutually entangle and draw one another;

they cannot escape this, yet within true emptiness, none of these three ever existed from the beginning. Although the three are originally one path, there are differences between their extensive and abbreviated formulations.
In essence, the Tathāgata taught the eighteen *dhātus* for those of dull faculties, the twelve *āyatanas* for those of middling faculties, and the five *skandhas* for those of sharp faculties;
thus, they differ because the teachings were imparted according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Contact is inexhaustible; Buddhists call this the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), which is what Mencius calls the "four limbs.

Phenomena (*dharma*) are matters; all phenomena arise from the mind. Buddhists call this the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), which is what Mencius refers to as the method of practicing the Way while awaiting destiny.
Chan Master Puan said: "It cannot be squeezed into a ball, nor can it be pushed aside..."
"Kai, why must you go to Nanyue or Tiantai? The gates of the six sense-faculties are places no one reaches;
it is only because they have been left untended that the barbarian monk has come all this way. Xu Shiying said, "If ordinary people have thought, they easily fall into the heterodox;
if they have no thought, they are like earth or wood. There must be thought that is not heterodox, and there must be a state of no-thought that is not like earth or wood."
If one understands this, then one knows that it is not easy for a bodhisattva to fully comprehend these thirteen "no-words.
"No-word" is the word for emptiness; to eliminate the root-knots of all existence, one must close the eyes and contemplate emptiness.
Contemplating the word [of emptiness] is wisdom itself. Ordinary people stir their thoughts and cling to existence, while those of the Lesser Vehicle stifle their thoughts and sink into emptiness.
"There is no ignorance, nor is there the end of ignorance; and so on, up to: there is no old age and death, nor is there the end of old age and death. Zongle said:
"This is the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). 'Ignorance' (*avidyā*) refers to delusive darkness;

it means that one lacks clear understanding regarding the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*). It does not mean a state of total unconsciousness, but rather refers to a forced, distorted cognition that runs contrary to reality."

Regarding "ignorance and so forth," the Bodhisattva contemplates this ignorance with the wisdom of *prajñā*, seeing that its nature is fundamentally empty and devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
therefore, it is said that "there is no ignorance, nor is there the extinction of ignorance. This applies even up to "no extinction of old age and death";
the meaning is the same as before, but while the beginning and end are mentioned, the middle is omitted. [The twelve links of dependent origination...]
The conditions are also called the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). First is ignorance (*avidyā*), also called affliction (*kleśa*).
Second is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), which refers to the performance of various karmas; these two links are the causes produced in the past.

Third is consciousness (*vijñāna*), which refers to the arising of deluded thoughts at the initial entry into the mother’s womb. Fourth is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), from which the various sense faculties (*indriya*) develop after entering the womb.
Five, form (*rūpa*): the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are formed within the womb. Six, contact (*sparśa*): after the formation of the embryo, the six sense bases encounter the six objects.
Seven, sensation (*vedanā*): this refers to the experiencing of worldly things, such as the pleasant and the unpleasant;
these five links are the fruits experienced in the present life. Eight, craving (*tṛṣṇā*): this refers to the greedy attachment to the five desires.
...and so forth. Ninth is *upādāna* (clinging), which refers to the arising of a mind of attachment toward various objects.
Tenth is *bhava* (existence), which refers to acting as the cause for outflowing (*āsrava*) states that can summon future results; these three links constitute the causes produced in the present.
Eleventh is *jāti* (birth), which refers to receiving a body composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in the future. Twelfth is...
"Old age and death" refers to the aging and dying of the future body; these two links are the fruits to be experienced in a future life.
These twelve links of dependent origination encompass the causes and effects of the three periods of time, revolving one after another in mutual dependence like a turning wheel that never ceases.
It is truly lamentable that all sentient beings are deluded and unaware of this. This is the root [text].
The realm observed by those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is that which Mahayana Bodhisattvas thoroughly illuminate as being entirely devoid of real nature;
therefore, it is said to be "non-existent. Guishan stated:
"The arising of the twelve links of dependent origination constitutes the ordinary person; the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination constitutes the sage."
Because emptiness is devoid of ordinary beings and sages, both arising and ceasing are absent.
The Buddha-ocean says: beginning with ignorance and ending with old age and death is the arising through dependent origination;
from the exhaustion of ignorance up to the exhaustion of old age and death is the cessation through dependent origination. "Exhaustion" is the meaning of "cessation."
Song Jingliao said: "Non-existence" refers to the contemplation of the gate of the forward flow of ignorance, which is called non-existent because it is ultimate emptiness.
"Exhaustion" refers to the contemplation of the gate of the reverse cessation of ignorance; because it is ultimate emptiness, there is nothing that can be exhausted.
The phrase "and so forth" is also an abbreviation; while the preceding mentions the first link and the following mentions the last link, the ten intermediate links can be inferred.
It is known by example that the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are the most detailed exposition of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The twelve links of dependent origination are the Western doctrine of the causes and effects of saṃsāra; they do not exist within the nature of a Bodhisattva.
Master Zhuzi had never fully investigated these conditions, and thus he disparaged the Western teachings on conditions and karma.

To refute Master Daxiong is an error. Those of the lower grade of Chan speak of saṃsāra, believing that if one’s single thought at the moment of death is unerring, one can enter a womb or seize another’s body to return and practice again.
Those of the higher grade of Chan do not speak of saṃsāra. Someone once asked Venerable Zhaozhou: "After you have lived for a hundred years, [what will become of you?]"
"Where does one go? Zhaozhou said, "After being burned by fire, it becomes a single stalk of reed.
This means that Master Zhaozhou did not speak of saṃsāra. Chan Master Chuan said, "This ceasing of the skin-bag; apart from this, there is no further obstruction.
Amidst the great embers of a blazing inferno, beyond the bright moon and the clear breeze—this is Chan Master Chuan."
The Master does not speak of saṃsāra; this is so even for those who have attained the heights of Chan, let alone for the Buddha.
Of the Buddha’s words, there is only the *Heart Sūtra*, which does not speak of saṃsāra, nor of suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path.
Zongle said: "There is no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path; this is the purity of the Four Noble Truths. Suffering refers to the fruit of suffering within birth and death;
accumulation refers to the afflictions and karma that cause suffering—these three are the phenomena of the mundane world. Cessation refers to the fruit of bliss in nirvana;
the path refers to the factors of enlightenment that bring about bliss—these two are the phenomena of the supramundane world. Thus he spoke.

Regarding the Four Noble Truths: it is intended to cause sentient beings to know suffering, sever the origin [of suffering], aspire toward cessation, and cultivate the path, thereby leaving suffering behind and attaining happiness.

This is the realm contemplated by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle; however, when Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas illuminate and realize this realm, they see that its very substance is empty and quiescent, and thus it is said to be "non-existent."
Song Jingliao said: "In this way, the Four Noble Truths are all non-existent within true emptiness.
However, the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are identical in meaning despite the difference in their names; they differ merely in terms of expansion and contraction.
Furthermore, they are taught repeatedly because the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings vary."

The character "Dao" (Way) refers precisely to precept, concentration, and wisdom; it should be examined in conjunction with the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*’s teaching that there is neither dharma nor non-dharma, otherwise one will ultimately have nothing to grasp.
There is no wisdom and no attainment.

Zongle said: "Wisdom" refers to the wisdom of *prajñā*. When a Mahayana Bodhisattva uses wisdom to illuminate objects, since the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the various dharmas such as the four truths (*catur-ārya-satya*) are non-existent, this constitutes the emptiness of both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*). Consequently, both object and wisdom vanish;
just as when the illness is cured, the medicine is forgotten, it is said that "there is neither wisdom nor attainment."
Song Jingliao said: "Not only are all the aforementioned phenomena non-existent within emptiness, but even the wisdom that knows emptiness cannot be apprehended.
Not only can the wisdom that knows emptiness not be apprehended, but even this principle of emptiness which is known likewise cannot be apprehended.
For the ultimate nature of the single truth is profoundly still and eternally quiescent; it does not depend upon cultivation or realization, and is utterly devoid of even a single [dharma]."
This is because of the Dharma. This concludes the preceding section and introduces the following one.

This fourth section states that within emptiness there are fundamentally no five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), yet it elaborates upon all phenomena (*dharma*) to bring the meaning of the previous three sections to completion.

Previously, it was said that "the five aggregates are all empty," which was spoken from the perspective of the person; here, it is said that "within emptiness there are no five aggregates, etc.," which is spoken from the perspective of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*).
It is said:
"Within true emptiness, there exists only the original nature and no other thing. Master Fu Daoshi said: "Once you have reached the shore, you do not need a boat.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "Bodhi is fundamentally no tree; the bright mirror is also not a stand. From the beginning..."
When there is not a single thing, where can dust and grime cling? Master Huanglong said: "Wherever there are a thousand rivers, there are a thousand moons;
where there are ten thousand miles of cloudless sky, there are ten thousand miles of heaven. Master Chuan said: "The sun and moon are newly forged; it is truly a vast universe.
If one says there is neither wisdom nor attainment, then one is like a bridge of wood or dead ashes—how could such a person be capable of awakening?

One should contemplate the line from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere," and one should also contemplate the two lines from the *Mahāśrī-vimalakīrti-prakṛti-prabhāsvara-parivarta* (The Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra):

"Though all illusions are exhausted, they do not enter into annihilation. From this, one will know that supreme, right enlightenment arises from the original nature as a spontaneous, empty, and luminous awareness.
Through initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), only delusion is extinguished, while fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) remains radiant and clear.
That this alone remains is precisely what is called the time of transcending emotions and casting off attachments. Initial awakening (*shikaku*) is humanity; original awakening (*hongaku*) is heaven.
When there is no intellect, one is human; when heaven is obliterated, one is established in certainty.
"Because there is nothing to be attained.
Zongle said: "This is a statement that concludes the preceding section and initiates the subsequent one.
Song Jingliao said: "'Nothing to be attained' refers back to the 'no attainment' mentioned in the preceding text. Because there is nothing to be attained..."
For this reason, Bodhisattvas rely on Prajñāpāramitā and other factors to attain the fruit of Nirvāṇa, which is the result of cessation;

likewise, the Buddhas of the three periods of time rely on Prajñāpāramitā and other factors to attain the fruit of Bodhi-wisdom. This is because all dharmas are fundamentally empty, as will be seen in detail below.
Because Bodhisattvas rely on the perfection of wisdom, their minds are without hindrance; because they are without hindrance, they have no fear;
they are far removed from all inverted dreams and delusions, and they attain ultimate Nirvana.
Wunianzi said: "The Bodhisattva and the Buddha represent the distinction between the sage and the ordinary person;
those who seek ultimate nirvana should recognize this for themselves.
Zongle said: "Bodhisattva refers to the person who relies [upon the path], while Prajñāpāramitā is..."

This is the Dharma upon which [the Bodhisattva] relies. When a Bodhisattva relies on this Dharma-gate of Prajñā to practice and study until their merit is perfected and the principle is revealed, they attain a mind free from the bonds of karma. Because there are no karmic bonds, there is no fear of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Since there is no fear of birth and death, there are no inverted afflictions (*kleśa*). Once these three obstacles are empty, the three virtues [are realized].
It is manifested as such, hence it is called ultimate *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* is a Sanskrit term;

*mahā-parinirvāṇa* is its Chinese translation, meaning "Great Extinction-Crossing. "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the *dharmakāya*; "extinction" (*nirodha*) refers to *vimukti*; and "crossing" (*pāra*) refers to *prajñā*.
These three virtues are not something separate; they are precisely the three obstructions when in a state of delusion, and the three virtues when awakened. That which is so-called is as follows:
Birth-and-death is itself the Dharma-body; afflictions are themselves prajñā; fetters and karma are themselves liberation.

Yet these very obstructions are themselves virtues; were it not for the merit of prajñā, they could not be manifested. This is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the clarity appears. Such is what is meant.
Worthy One, it is said: "There is no fear" means that externally there is no fear of demonic adversaries, which signifies the cessation of adverse conditions.
"Far removed from inverted dreams" means that internally there is no arrival of delusive obstructions, which signifies the exhaustion of evil causes.

Ancient Yun said: "By relying on the wisdom of wondrous emptiness, one realizes that the nature of objects and the mind are perfectly constant from moment to moment and ultimately perfected in every particle of dust.
Thus, karmic bonds and afflictions are themselves liberation; therefore, there is no obstruction. The path of suffering is itself the Dharma-body;

therefore, there is no fear. Afflictions are themselves bodhi; therefore, one is free from inverted dreams and delusions. The three obstructions are not abandoned, yet they are abandoned; the three virtues are not..."
It is perfectly round, and its quiescent extinction flows into *nirvāṇa* spontaneously.
Song Jinglian said: "Guà" (罣) means like a thread suspended; "ài" (礙) means like a stone obstructing. It signifies fear, distant separation, and liberation.
"Diān" (顛) refers to the crown of the head; "diāndǎo" (顛倒) refers to being inverted or hanging upside down. In sleep it is a dream; in awakening—
It is the ultimate exhaustion and cessation of conceptualization. In Sanskrit, *nirvāṇa* means "perfectly pure.
By relying on this Dharma, the Bodhisattva cultivates sublime conduct, penetrates the vision of the purity of self-nature, and realizes entry into true emptiness.
Therefore, the mind is without hindrance; because the mind is without hindrance, naturally there is no fear, and one is far removed from inverted thoughts and delusions.
This is the moment of ultimate, perfect purity.
When there is no fear, the anxieties and afflictions of birth and death cannot enter; this is where Liu Tiehan’s daily engagement with Buddhist scriptures resides.
○ Dreaming of wandering in Huaxu and dreaming of the Duke of Zhou—though these were sages, they could not avoid them.
One who can be free from dream-thoughts surpasses even the Three Kings; though one may contemplate throughout the entire night, even a sage cannot be free from conceptualization.

To be utterly remote from dream-imaginations is what constitutes the supramundane dharma. Regarding the two characters "Nirvana" (涅槃), worldly people mistakenly believe it means death, but this is not so.
In the preface to the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (圓覺經) by Prime Minister Pei, it says: "Quiescence is eternal."
Because it is blissful, it is called *nirvāṇa*. Xu Shiying says: "The Sanskrit term *nirvāṇa* here means 'unconditioned' (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, *nirvāṇa* signifies immovability and the state of being unconditioned. This 'unconditioned' is what Yang Xiong referred to as 'mysterious silence.
It is free from terror because it abides in change; it is free from dreams and desires because it abides in the eternal. It is said to be non-existent.
Those who are free from fear, detached from dreams and thoughts, and whose minds are without hindrance are able [to realize this];
those whose minds have hindrances are not.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Bodhi. Zongle said: "The 'three periods' refer to the past, future, and present.
'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi' is a Chinese translation meaning 'Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Enlightenment. This term does not apply solely to Bodhisattvas..."
This is the cultivation and realization through which all Buddhas have cultivated Prajñā and attained perfect enlightenment.
"Anuttara" means "unsurpassed"; "samyak" means "right";
"sam" means "equal"; and "bodhi" means "awakening. Thus, it is "unsurpassed, right, and equal awakening."
It is awakening (*bodhi*).
Song Jingliao said: "The three periods refer to the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*, the present *Bhadrakalpa*, and the future *Tārakakalpa*.
The Sanskrit term for Buddha is translated here as 'awakening' (*jue*). Awakening is the opposite of delusion; it is seen through the awakening of the Buddha."
Regarding the delusion of sentient beings, the Buddhas state that within the three periods of time there are not merely one, but a thousand Buddhas each.
The Buddhas of the three periods rely upon this single gate; it is said that there is no divergent path.
*A* in Sanskrit means "no"; *anuttara* in Sanskrit means "supreme"; *samyak* in Sanskrit means "correct"; *saṃbodhi* in Sanskrit [means]... [text fragment ends].

The equality of bodhi has been explained above; the Buddhas of the three periods of time also rely upon this Dharma to cultivate wondrous practices, penetratingly perceive the purity of self-nature, and enter into true emptiness to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This fifth section cites the conduct of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to substantiate this, showing that one realizes the truth by relying on prajñā.
That which is empty cannot be grasped; the meaning of the five aggregates is thus exhausted without remainder.
"Unsurpassed, Right, Perfect Enlightenment" corresponds to the "sagehood achieved through the wisdom of the written word"; "the sage who cannot be fathomed" corresponds to Mencius’s "sage";
and "that which is called spiritual" corresponds to the "clarity, intelligence, and sagely wisdom that reach the virtue of Heaven" in the *Zhongyong*.
Knowing this, one understands that while the Buddha and our Confucian tradition are identical in essence, they differ in their application. Therefore,
know that Prajñāpāramitā is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed mantra,
and the mantra unequaled by any other.
Zongle said: "The former is an explicit exposition of Prajñā, while the latter is a secret exposition of Prajñā;

this is because the faculties of sentient beings differ, and thus their points of entry vary. As for the four kinds of mantras, it is said that the efficacy of Prajñā can shatter demonic obstacles, hence it is called the 'Great Divine Mantra';
it can extinguish the darkness of ignorance, hence it is called the 'Great Illuminating Mantra'; it can reveal..."
The ultimate principle is called the "Unsurpassed Mantra. The fruit of supreme, wondrous enlightenment, having no equal, is called the "Unequaled Mantra.

Song Jingliao said: "Therefore, we know" serves to conclude the preceding and initiate what follows. "Mantra" refers to the secret words spoken by the Buddha, which is the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
"Spiritual" (*shen*) is a term for that which is subtle, wondrous, and unfathomable; "luminous" (*ming*) refers to that which reflects and illuminates without obscuration.
This is what is meant by "Great," which refers to that which is not comparable to small deities or small wisdom;
it is unsurpassed and beyond further addition or transcendence; it is peerless, solitary, and without equal.

Since it has already been called "Great" to signify its ultimate limit, the repetition of "unsurpassed" and "peerless" is intended to profoundly manifest that the Prajñāpāramitā is vast and boundless, infinitely expansive.
Only the boundless, ultimate void can suffice to embody this.
Both the Daoist and Buddhist traditions possess incantations (*dhāraṇī*), whereas Confucianism does not;

yet, among the people of Zhou there was an official charged with incantations, among the people of Qin there were texts for incantations against Chu, and in the *Mao Shih* there is the passage on "producing the three substances to perform incantations."
From the time of the Han dynasty, there were incantations involving wooden figures that brought about the calamity of Jiang Chong;

during the Liang dynasty, there were incantations involving wax effigies that resulted in the grievous injustice suffered by Prince Zhaoming. Thus, the use of incantations in the Middle Kingdom has long existed.
When seeking their application, these incantations are so divinely subtle that they can command spirits and deities, manipulate wind and rain, and subjugate all things.
That dragons and tigers exist only in the Western Regions to this day is, indeed, a principle within heaven and earth that remains inexplicable.
Formerly, while in Guanzhong, I heard a scholar say that in years past a Western monk came here and, by means of incantations, turned a large stone into ash;
when he wished to slaughter an ox, he recited a mantra and the ox died immediately, after which it was skinned and eaten.
Master Changshui said: "The bitter plum is boundless; turning one's head is the shore.
It can eliminate all suffering; this is truly not false. Zongle said:
"This concludes the function of Prajñā: its vastness in eliminating suffering and attaining joy is definitively unimpeded."
Gu Yun said: "To sigh that [the world] is not empty and to exhort others to practice the pāramitās—this is the ultimate true Dharma-boat for crossing over the realms of suffering.
May all sentient beings swiftly give rise to the ground of wisdom.
Song Jinglian said: "To be able to eliminate all suffering is precisely to cross over all suffering; this is not something realized by those who have not attained the True Emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."
"It cannot be done," [he said], fearing that sentient beings would not believe him. Thus, having stated it in the first section, he reiterates it here;
and by further following this with the words "truly and not falsely," he means that [the teaching] can certainly eliminate suffering.
How great is his true compassion for sentient beings! This sixth section follows from the preceding text.
The praise and chanting of the wondrous, true emptiness of Prajñā have been so extensive that, from this point upward, it is generally termed "Manifest Prajñā.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "In delusion, a Buddha is a sentient being; in awakening, a sentient being is a Buddha. Its pivot lies therein.
That I have no difficulties is why this Buddha has uttered this sigh of truth and non-falsity.
Therefore, he spoke the Prajñāpāramitā mantra, which is spoken as follows:
*gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
Zongle said: "The above is the *Guhyaprajñā*; this is one of the five types [of terms] that are not translated.
For mantras are the secret language of the Buddha, not something known by ordinary beings of the lower realms. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states:

'Mantras are the names and titles of ghost-king deities; by invoking the name of such a king, the subordinate chieftains and generals are brought under control, and thus one is able to subdue all malevolent spirits.'"
Furthermore, "dhāraṇī" (zhòu) means a vow (*praṇidhāna*). It is like the *gonglo* (sire-wasp) that "incants" the *mingling* (caterpillar), vowing for it to become its own kind.
When Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak dhāraṇīs, they make vows for all sentient beings, saying: "May they attain perfect enlightenment just as I have.
For one who can recite this dhāraṇī, there shall be no unfulfilled vow.
The Venerable One said: "If one wishes to provide a forced explanation, *gate* means 'crossing over' (*tāraṇa*), which refers to the function of profound wisdom;
it is repeated to indicate the place reached. *Pāragate* means 'crossing over oneself and crossing over others. *Pārasaṃgate*:
*pāra* means 'the other shore,' which is the destination reached by crossing over. *Pārasaṃgate*..."
“Saṃgha” means “totality” or “universality”; it refers to the universal deliverance of both oneself and others, such that all reach the further shore.
As for “bodhi,” what kind of further shore does it denote? It refers to the state of Great Bodhi.
As for “sambhava,” this is translated as “swiftly”; it means that the aforementioned [qualities] are swiftly brought to fulfillment.
Gushan said: "The secret words of all Buddhas do not require explanation; as a general rule, such esoteric expressions are left untranslated.
One should simply seek their ultimate meaning, which is merely a cryptic statement of the previously mentioned mind of non-attainment in Prajñā."

The Buddhist discourse on nature differs from the Confucian discourse on nature; the Confucians discuss nature in terms of principle (*li*), whereas the Buddhists discuss..."

Nature is described in terms of its vacuity, spirituality, and cognitive awareness; yet, when one investigates the reason why it is vacuous, spiritual, and aware, it is because it is the *shen* (spirit).
If a person can penetrate and resolve the meaning of this word "spirit," then they will know that what the Buddhist school calls the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body) is this very thing;
the master of the house is this very thing; and the indestructible diamond body (*vajrakāya*) is this very thing. This is the fundamental source.
This is what is meant by "the face as it is when coming forth. As for the question, "Before my parents were born, who was I?
this is likewise the case among our Confucian scholars. The *Daiji* says, "The spirit of the mind is called sagehood";
Zisi says, "Ultimate sincerity is like the divine"; and Mencius says, "The spirit of the mind is called sagehood," while Zisi also says, "Ultimate sincerity is like the divine."
Mencius said, "That which is preserved is spiritual. Zhouzi said, "Spirituality responds, therefore it is wondrous. This is also the case in Daoism;
the *Laozi* says, "The primal spirit," and the *Zhuangzi* says, "The essence of the ultimate Way: embrace the spirit and remain still.
Wei Boyang said, "The True Man dwells in the deep abyss," and Zhang Pingshu said, "The infant enters the mechanism of the sage."
All these are this very thing. By analogy, those who rode the dragon at Mount Dinghu rode upon this; those who transformed into cranes in Liaodong transformed into this;
the one who faced the wall at Mount Song faced this; and the one who slept soundly on Mount Hua slept upon this.
Among all things in heaven and earth, the Way is most subtle and most wondrous. Its pivot lies within me; who else could apply it?
I can only regret that my hair is burdened by various labors and my mind tossed by the winds and waves; could this not be what is called "a dream within a dream" from which one has not yet awakened?
Alas! On what day shall the traveler from afar return? Looking up at the heavens with a smile, the Dweller Without Thought records this.
